proposedSourceScopeReplacement: Actual 470-page university PDF: title/licence, preface xi–xiii, introduction 1–4, political history 96–100 (PDF 116–120) and language documentation 118–121 (PDF 138–141). Selected pages only; ceremonial appendices and later extinction chapter are not used.

claimBlock.suggestedSection: A surviving written record of the language
claimBlock.text: Hann describes a 1688 letter by Apalachee chiefs, preserved with a contemporary Spanish translation, as central evidence for studying the language. He cautions that Indigenous words recorded by Spaniards were not necessarily Apalachee.
claimBlock.sourceLocator: Hann, printed 118 (PDF 138), especially the first two paragraphs

inspection.actualPages: Actual printed 118–121 (PDF 138–141), read from the already inspected university edition; original PDF and a selected language extraction preserved privately.
inspection.method: pypdf extraction read in full for those four pages, including chapter opening, historical comparative discussions and interpreter passages.
inspection.evidence: Printed 118 identifies the 1688 chiefs’ letter, Fray Marcelo de San Joseph’s contemporary Spanish translation and later publication/English translation through Spanish. The same page warns that words used by Spaniards about Apalachee could instead be Arawak or Timucua.
inspection.limits: The proposed block does not assert this remains the only surviving text today, current language vitality, extinction of a people, an independent reading or translation of the original letter, or a definitive modern linguistic classification. Later discussion of comparative relationships is not adopted as present consensus. Ceremonial manuscript references are not reproduced, explained or counted separately.
